references.title: Trudel G. et al., Hemolysis contributes to anemia during long-duration space flight, Nature Medicine, 2022
references.claim: In 14 astronauts on 6-month missions, the body destroyed 54% more red blood cells than on the ground (≈ 3 million/s instead of 2) throughout the mission; reversible 3–4 months after return.
references.usedFor: Slow hemoglobin / hematocrit decline in the generator; cardio layer
references.status: Institution press summary (Ottawa Hospital) read; Nature Medicine article not re-read

references.title: Okada A. et al., Bisphosphonate use may reduce the risk of urolithiasis in astronauts on long-term spaceflights, JBMR Plus, 2022 (PMID 35079672)
references.claim: 17 ISS astronauts (6 months). ARED-only group: urinary calcium rising from D15–D30 and elevated urinary bone resorption markers (NTX, HP); ARED + alendronate group: no rise. High risk of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones.
references.usedFor: Daily urine (calcium, NTX); rule “rising calcium → hydration + kidney scan”

references.title: Smith S.M., Calcium and Bone Metabolism During Spaceflight, NASA Johnson Space Center (NTRS 20100030546)
references.claim: Increased urinary calcium excretion is a major contributor to in-flight kidney stone risk; blood calcium stays regulated.
references.usedFor: Why calcium is tracked in URINE rather than blood

references.title: Thamer S., Buckey J.C., First void urinary calcium for tracking bone loss and kidney stone risk in space, Aerosp. Med. Hum. Perform. 93(7), 2022
references.claim: First-morning urinary calcium allows real-time tracking of bone loss and stone risk in flight.
references.usedFor: Justifies the daily first-morning urine sample (realistic in flight)

references.title: LeBlanc A. et al., Bisphosphonates as a supplement to exercise to protect bone during long-duration spaceflight, Osteoporos. Int. 24(7):2105-14, 2013 (NASA–JAXA)
references.claim: 7 ISS astronauts (5.5 months), alendronate 70 mg/week + ARED: the combination attenuates the decline of nearly all bone indices, compared with 18 + 11 astronauts on exercise alone.
references.usedFor: Hip ground routine (“discuss bisphosphonates with the flight surgeon”). REPLACES the incorrect attribution to the V1 4027 rationale

references.title: LeBlanc A., Bisphosphonate as a Countermeasure to Space Flight-Induced Bone Loss (NTRS 20090041838)
references.claim: On Mir and the ISS (~171-day flights), over 90% of astronauts lost at least 5% at one or more bone sites, and 40% at least 10%.
references.status: Excerpt read. NB: the sheet's figure “< 5% hip loss with ARED” remains UNSOURCED

references.title: Fall D.A. et al., Optic nerve sheath diameter and spaceflight: defining shortcomings and future directions, npj Microgravity 8:42, 2022
references.claim: Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD), measured by ultrasound on the ground and in microgravity, serves as an indirect marker of intracranial pressure. Up to 60% of long-duration astronauts develop neuro-ocular changes (SANS). Published measurements are heterogeneous: the review calls for standardization.
references.usedFor: Scanner “optic nerve sheath” metric; limitation to display (indirect, noisy marker)

references.title: NASA, Vision Changes on Space Station (Science in Space, July 2025)
references.claim: Photo and description of an eye ultrasound performed by astronauts on the ISS; SANS = optic disc edema and globe flattening.
references.usedFor: Proof that ocular ultrasound is ALREADY done onboard (pitch)

references.title: “Bone ultrasound” review (PMC12082152) + Shung, Diagnostic Ultrasound (2005)
references.claim: Ultrasound imaging of bone is traditionally limited: high acoustic impedance and density → strong reflection, absorption, scattering, poor penetration. Bone attenuation ≈ 6–9 dB/(MHz·cm) versus 0.5 for liver.
references.usedFor: Why the scanner does NOT measure bone density (v3.2); “honesty” slide

references.title: AGBRESA (Artificial Gravity Bed Rest – ESA), DLR :envihab, Cologne, 2019 — NASA / DLR / ESA
references.claim: First joint DLR–ESA–NASA bed-rest study (60 days, 2019) testing a short-arm human centrifuge as a microgravity countermeasure: 30 min/day at 1 g at the center of mass, continuous or intermittent; 960 runs, 10 stopped (discomfort), mostly no motion sickness.
references.usedFor: Real-world basis for the “onboard centrifuge” hypothesis [H]
references.status: DLR, NASA and Frett 2020 (PLOS ONE) pages read

references.title: Oh H.S.-H. et al., Organ aging signatures in the plasma proteome track health and disease, Nature 624:164–172, 2023
references.claim: Using organ-specific plasma proteins, age was estimated for 11 organs in 5,676 adults; ~20% of the population has an organ with strongly accelerated aging; an “older” heart multiplies the risk of heart failure.
references.usedFor: Scientific backing for the “age per organ” idea. Our age gap [H] is a much simpler indicator, not this method

references.title: Fleg J.L. et al., Accelerated longitudinal decline of aerobic capacity in healthy older adults, Circulation 112:674-682, 2005
references.claim: Longitudinal decline in peak VO₂: 3–6% per decade in the twenties and thirties, accelerating each decade (> 20% after 70), steeper in men from age 40. “~10%/decade” is the common simplification.
references.usedFor: Terrestrial heart aging rate for the age gap [H]

references.title: MINOS prospective study (725 men aged 50–85, 90 months); MrOS (Cawthon 2009, JBMR)
references.claim: Total hip density loss ≈ 0.5%/year and femoral neck ≈ 0.3%/year in men over 50; MrOS: ~0.3%/year at the femoral neck (men ≥ 65), accelerating with age.
references.usedFor: Terrestrial hip rate for the age gap [H]

references.title: Meta-analysis of 47 cross-sectional studies (≈ 25 vs 75 years, PMC10069966); Cameron 2019 (thigh MRI, 70+)
references.claim: Muscle size loss ≈ 0.4%/year on average between 25 and 75 depending on the muscle group; ≈ 1%/year for the thigh after 70 (−5% in 5 years on MRI).
references.usedFor: Terrestrial thigh/calf rate for the age gap [H]

references.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief — Exercise (Dec. 2023)
references.claim: On the ISS: ~600 min of exercise per week; prescription ≈ 30 min aerobic (T2, CEVIS, 70–100% HRmax or peak VO₂) + 30–60 min resistance training on ARED (squat, calf raises, deadlift). Recommendation: at least 3 sessions per week > 70% HRmax, > 20 min.
